title: Failure is Feedback: History-Aware Backtracking for Agentic Traversal in Multimodal Graphs
one_liner: Search a linked document graph more intelligently by treating dead ends as evidence about where not to go next, then spend extra reasoning cost only when that evidence justifies it.
lead: This paper studies open-domain retrieval over large document graphs containing paragraphs, tables, and images. The task is not only to score one item at a time. The system must move through a graph, decide which node to visit next, and recover when earlier hops were poor choices. Failure is Feedback turns that search into a sequential decision problem where bad paths are not discarded. They are stored as clues that shape later backtracking and later spending on heavier reasoning.

problem.h2: Why graph retrieval needs recovery, not only ranking
paras: In a linked document collection, the correct answer may sit several hops away from the starting node. A system must decide which neighbor to inspect next, which evidence to keep, and when to turn back. If one early hop is weak, the rest of the path can become wasteful because later nodes are chosen from the wrong local neighborhood.

Many graph retrieval methods rely on one similarity rule or one fixed traversal plan. That is limiting because the meaning of a good hop changes with context, and because dead ends should teach the system something about which branches are unlikely to help.

callout.html: Treat failed traversals as information, because a dead end says not only that one path failed but also which related moves are now less promising.

panels.title: 1. Start in a large graph
panels.viz_args: paragraphs, tables, and images linked together
panels.caption: The answer may require several hops across different content types.

panels.title: 2. Follow one path
panels.caption: The current evidence suggests one route, but some hops are still uncertain.

panels.title: 3. Hit a dead end
panels.viz_args: relevant answer not found on this branch
panels.caption: A failure reveals that the branch was weak, but it also reveals which local cues misled the search.

panels.title: 4. Backtrack with memory
panels.caption: The next move is changed by what failed before, so the system avoids repeating the same weak pattern.

panels.title: 5. Spend extra reasoning only when needed
panels.caption: Heavier reasoning is used only after cheaper traversal evidence says the extra cost is justified.

steps.text: The system chooses one hop at a time through a multimodal graph, because each new node changes which future hops are worth considering.
When a branch does not lead to the answer, the system stores what it tried and why it failed so that the same mistake is less likely to recur.
Backtracking does not simply reset the state. It returns with extra context about the failed branch, so the next branch choice is informed by negative evidence.
The orchestrator uses cheap traversal steps first and pays for heavier reasoning only when the failure history suggests that the extra cost may change the outcome.

steps.b: Stop when evidence is good enough.
steps.text: The search ends when the system has gathered a sufficiently strong answer path, because endless exploration adds cost without useful new evidence.

paras: The paper changes graph retrieval from fixed forward traversal into a history-aware search process where failure explicitly shapes later navigation and later reasoning spend.
object.object: the traversal policy over a multimodal document graph

hidden.name: expected value of the next branch after accounting for past failures
paras: The main hidden quantity is how promising each next branch remains after you take earlier failures into account. Two branches may look equally relevant from the current node, yet one may repeat the same weak evidence pattern that already failed earlier.

The paper estimates that hidden value by combining current context with traversal history. That helps because negative evidence shrinks the search space: once one style of branch has failed, related branches deserve a lower rank unless new context changes the picture.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the parts of search state that tell the system whether a branch deserves another try.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is whether a branch is still worth exploring after you remember what failed before, because negative evidence should narrow the search.
The method values branches through a history-aware traversal policy that treats earlier failures as informative signals for future path choice and reasoning spend.

paras: Ordinary backtracking throws away too much information. It returns to an earlier node, but it does not preserve which cues led the search down a useless path. That means the next choice can repeat a closely related mistake because the system has forgotten what the dead end taught it. History-aware backtracking keeps the failure context, so the next step is guided both by what currently looks relevant and by what has already proven unhelpful.

The cost-aware control also matters. Heavy reasoning can rescue difficult cases, but using it everywhere wastes compute on easy hops. The orchestrator therefore delays that cost until cheaper search evidence suggests it is needed. This helps because the system spends more only when failures indicate that simple traversal is no longer enough.

stages.s: pay for heavier reasoning only if justified

math.h2: Score the next branch using success value, failure memory, and cost
math.words: A simple summary is to prefer branches that still look useful under the current context, subtract a penalty when they resemble earlier failures, and subtract the extra reasoning cost needed to pursue them.
symbols: overall value of choosing one next branch
how well the current graph state supports that branch
how strongly earlier dead ends suggest this branch will also fail
added reasoning spend required to evaluate that branch

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Branch A looks relevant now, so current evidence is 8.
It closely resembles a path that already failed, so failure penalty is 5.
It also needs extra heavy reasoning with cost 2.
Branch B has current evidence 7, failure penalty 1, and extra cost 1.
Branch B wins because it offers a cleaner new direction after accounting for what earlier failures already taught the system.

math.note: The paper uses a richer traversal mechanism than this line, but the line captures the main idea: the next move should be judged by present relevance, earlier failures, and added search cost together.

charts.title: Static traversal with uniform scoring
charts.note: A static policy struggles because it keeps treating failures as isolated accidents instead of as evidence that should change later search.

charts.title: Failure is Feedback
charts.note: The paper reports a better tradeoff between answer quality and answering cost because history-aware backtracking avoids repeated weak branches and reserves heavier reasoning for harder cases.

items.b: Failure memory can become too pessimistic.
items.html: If the system punishes every similar branch too strongly, it may skip the correct answer path because some useful branches superficially resemble earlier failures.

items.b: The graph may hide good links.
items.html: A weak graph structure can block retrieval no matter how smart the traversal policy is, because the right node may not be reachable through the provided links.

items.b: Cheap early hops may under-sample hard cases.
items.html: If the system waits too long before using heavier reasoning, it can remain trapped in shallow evidence because the cheap traversal policy never sees the cue that would justify more effort.
The method is strongest when failure history is informative but not overwhelming, because then backtracking rules out repeated bad patterns without hiding fresh useful branches.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a linked graph of short passages, tables, and images where some answer paths require two or three hops. Create several distractor branches that look locally relevant but end in dead ends. Compare a forward-only search policy, a plain backtracking policy, and a history-aware backtracking policy with a budget on expensive reasoning calls.

The demo should show that history-aware backtracking reaches the answer more often with similar or lower spend because it learns from failed paths instead of repeatedly revisiting their close variants. It should also show when heavier reasoning is triggered and whether that extra cost was justified by a later improvement in the found answer path.
demo.closing: A convincing demo must prove that dead ends improve later search when their history is retained, because recovery should use failure as evidence instead of treating it as wasted work.
